extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers of Popular Science Monthly and public-health/interested lay readers
extracted.subtask_description: Popular-science guidance on (1) causes, classification, health implications, and prevention of dreaming/poor sleep, and (2) sanitary relations of soil, soil-moisture vs groundwater, and practical hygiene implications for infectious disease. The content is aimed at informing lay and public-health-minded readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural (complete) sleep
rubrics_metrics.description: "Natural sleep is simultaneous sleep of all the faculties of body and mind"; when sleep is natural (complete) dreaming is improbable or impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To secure natural sleep, order life so higher intellectual powers, automatic activities, the senses, muscular system, and viscera (principally the stomach) are all ready and able to sleep at the same time; make sleep periodic with rhythmical regularity. The measure of dreaming is inversely the measure of the integrity of sleep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of separate/faculty-specific sleeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Habitual allowing of some faculties to remain awake while others sleep (separate sleep) produces dreaming and is injurious to health: "A dreamer who is not unhealthy ... must have formed the habit of allowing his faculties to sleep separately."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid lifestyles that keep some centers active (e.g., brain work with little muscular exercise). Prevent the habit where centers of the brain take rest independently; otherwise partial sleep leads to unrest, dozing, and frequent dreaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dreaming as indicator of health/cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent or elaborate dreaming suggests impaired health or lack of cohesion among intellectual faculties: "A great dreamer can not be in good health."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use frequency and character of dreams (especially persistent/nightly vivid dreams) as a clue to mental/physical condition; beware that chronic partial sleep may lead to daytime disorganization of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity vs coherence of dreams
rubrics_metrics.description: Intensity without coherence in dreams is worse than equally vivid dreaming with more connectedness of thought: "Intensity without coherence is, as a rule, worse..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the seriousness of dreaming for health, consider both vividness and coherence — chaotic intense dreams (incoherent) are more injurious than vivid but connected dreams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dreams are recollections from stored impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Dreams are re-collections: pictures, thoughts, and impressions previously recorded by the brain are brought out and recombined; little is truly 'original' in dreams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To alter the character of future dreams, attend to the material stored in youth and adulthood — feed the mind with wholesome, healthy impressions; many dream elements are unconsciously accumulated and later reproduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of dreams (four classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dreams may be divided into four classes: 1) those of the present; 2) those of the past; 3) those of the future; 4) inchoate dreams (heapings together of inchoate ideas without time, order, or reason).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these classes diagnostically: each class has characteristic causes and implications for the sleeper's mental state (see individual entries on present/past/future/inchoate dreams).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dreams of the present as sign of jaded/lethargic memory-faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: When recent impressions are used as dream-material, the dream-making faculty is either jaded/exhausted or lethargic, producing dreams built from immediately previous attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dreams of the present are often tumultuous or oppressive and indicate overburdened recollecting faculties; distinguish lethargy (slow progression, fatigue) from exhaustion (tumultuous, oppressive, worry-like dreams). Consider these dreams as valuable clews to mind-state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dreams of the past and future indicate interest levels and anticipations
rubrics_metrics.description: Dreams of the past often occur when present interests are low (e.g., aging); dreams of the future are mostly anticipations/forebodings arising from present affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret frequent past-dreaming as a tendency toward retrospection or waning vitality; interpret future-oriented dreams as imagination's forecast of desired or dreaded outcomes rather than prophecy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inchoate/fragmentary dreams reflect sensory over-excitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Disconnected, fantastical, or delirium-like dreams (the fourth class) often follow undue excitement of the organs of sense immediately before going to bed (theatre, music, novels, dissipating scenes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These dreams are common but usually not of major health concern and can be obviated by giving the mind regular, methodized work and avoiding stimulating sensory input close to bedtime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of dream content via lifelong material-management
rubrics_metrics.description: While the will cannot call up or prevent particular dreams at will, the making of dreams is largely under the control of the will through the materials one accumulates over life: 'he who would dream pleasantly... must see to the material with which he stores his mind in youth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps: cultivate wholesome, pure mental impressions from youth; in adult life engage in wholesome occupations and reading to accumulate better dream-material for later years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical remedies to reduce distressing dreams
rubrics_metrics.description: To reduce inchoate or distressing dreams, give the mind regular, methodized work and lower excitement before bed; a practical remedy is reading aloud a not very exciting but interesting book for half an hour before retiring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to occupy the mind with a subject to shut out troublesome imaginings and train the senses to disregard externals when composing oneself for sleep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure peaceful and 'negative' conditions for sleep
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid external stimuli making themselves 'the pegs on which to hang a dream'; train senses to disregard external impressions and secure peaceful, neutral conditions for sleep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice resolving for several nights to ignore external impressions; reduce sensory excitement immediately before bed (no late theatre, exciting novels, or music).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish soil-moisture from ground-water
rubrics_metrics.description: Two degrees of soil moisture: (1) soil-moisture (air and water both occupy pores) and (2) ground-water (pores filled with water excluding air).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the level of ground-water as an index of the rhythm of soil-moisture in overlying strata; the sanitary effects depend on moisture in overlying strata rather than groundwater per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soil moisture (overlying strata) influences typhus/cholera prevalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Coincidence observed between ground-water/soil-moisture and typhoid/cholera fluctuations; variations in soil saturation of overlying strata affect epidemic patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume groundwater itself is causal; investigate moisture and processes in overlying layers. Artificially raising or lowering groundwater may not change epidemic prevalence unless overlying strata moisture changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cholera and typhus seasonality linked to soil saturation/rainfall
rubrics_metrics.description: Cholera and typhus in different locales fluctuate inversely with annual amount of rain and soil-saturation (e.g., Indian observations and European cities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use local patterns of rainfall and soil-moisture to anticipate epidemic seasonality; compare cities with different rainfall to interpret epidemic differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider both water and air as possible vehicles for epidemic influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Either air or water (or both) may convey epidemic influence from soil; the 'drinking-water theory' is not conclusively proven for diseases like typhus/cholera.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design investigations that can isolate air vs water exposure; public-health measures should not rely solely on water-protection theory because epidemics have occurred despite pure imported water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain soil organisms (e.g., malarial bacillus) require air
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bacillus malariae is 'preeminently an air-living organism' and cannot live without air; malarial poison not communicated to standing water over malarious mud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hygienic measures must consider organism-specific ecology (air-loving vs water-tolerant) when assessing transmission routes and remediation strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microbial survival in water depends on purity and available nutrients
rubrics_metrics.description: Naegeli: contagion-fungi keep activity in water only a short time; purer water contains less food and removes them by exhaustion; in clear spring-water they are removed quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing waterborne risk, consider water purity and nutrient content; pure spring water reduces persistence of many contagion-fungi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical observation favors airborne transmission in some epidemics
rubrics_metrics.description: Many cases exist where cholera/typhus ran their course without use of local water as drinking-water, but none where local air was excluded while local water used — suggesting air may play a dominant role in some outbreaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for airborne exposure in epidemic investigations and control measures; do not assume waterborne transmission solely from correlation with local water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide pure and abundant water regardless of transmission theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if water is not the primary vector in some epidemics, pure and abundant water is necessary for cleanliness, food, sick and well, and as a public-health good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-health policy should ensure ample clean water supply as both a protective and hygienic necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate mycological/microbiological findings cautiously into hygiene
rubrics_metrics.description: Mycology has produced hygienically important findings, but hygiene should not be reduced solely to microscopic study; the hygienist still has broader duties beyond laboratory work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use laboratory results (e.g., organism requirements) as tools but maintain a broader hygienic perspective — practical application (like Lister's use by surgeons) is required to make lab findings useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ventilation/dilution versus concentration of filth
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent greater filth in villages is often dilution by scattering (air exposure) whereas cities concentrate filth; ventilation of manure-heaps in country effects salutary dilution, while in cities filth is often enclosed and connected to houses by pipes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanitary practice should favor exposure/ventilation of waste materials (allowing dilution and aeration) rather than enclosing and hiding filth near dwellings. Cleanly kept houses are healthier than dirty ones everywhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume extreme concentration makes filth harmless
rubrics_metrics.description: Although some ferments are prevented by high concentration (e.g., fruit in concentrated syrup), hygiene has yet to determine how concentrated filth must be to prevent ferments contributing to cholera/typhus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on concentration as a sanitation strategy for dangerous wastes; empirical determination is needed before concluding concentrated filth is safe.
